questions.q: A charge is placed in a uniform electric field of strength E. In which direction does the constant force F = qE act on a positive charge and on a negative charge?
options: On both charges the force acts in the direction of the field
The force on a positive charge is in the direction of the field, and the force on a negative charge is opposite to the field direction
The force on a positive charge is opposite to the field, and the force on a negative charge is in the direction of the field
The direction depends only on the strength of the field, not the sign of the charge
questions.explanation: If a space contains a uniform field, a charge placed in it experiences a constant electric force F = qE. The direction of the force on a positive charge is in the direction of the field, and the force on a negative charge is opposite to the field direction. Because the force is constant, the acceleration is constant (F = ma). Always state the sign of the charge and the field direction together.

questions.q: Two metal plates a few centimetres apart are connected to the terminals of a battery, so the lines of electric field between the plates are evenly spaced. What does this even spacing of the field lines indicate?
options: The field strength is greatest near the positive plate and weakest near the negative plate
The strength of the field is constant between the plates — a uniform electric field
The field lines curve from one plate to the other
The field reverses direction halfway between the plates
questions.explanation: When two metal plates are connected to a battery, the lines of electric field in the space between them are evenly spaced, that is, the value of the strength of the field is constant. This is called a uniform electric field. The battery transfers electrons from one plate, making it positive, onto the other, making it negative.

questions.q: Equating the two expressions for work done on a charge between parallel plates, qEd = qV, leads to which result for the electric field strength, and what two equivalent units does it give?
options: E = qd, in coulombs per metre or joules per volt
E = V/d, giving electric field strength two equivalent units: newtons per coulomb or volts per metre
E = Vd, in volt-metres only
E = d/V, in metres per volt or coulombs per newton
questions.explanation: Work done is W = qV and also W = Fd = qE × d, where d is the separation of the plates. Equating qE × d = q × V and cancelling the charge q gives E = V/d. This provides an alternative unit for electric field of volts per metre, so electric field strength has two equivalent units: newtons per coulomb or volts per metre.

questions.q: What is the strength of the electric field between two parallel plates 5.0 cm apart connected to a 100 V DC supply?
questions.explanation: Convert the plate separation to metres (5.0 cm = 5.0 × 10⁻² m) before dividing. Using volts per metre makes it very easy to determine the strength of a uniform electric field: E = V/d = 2000 V m⁻¹ (equivalently 2000 N C⁻¹).

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a voltage drop of 100 V between two plates in an electron gun. How fast is the electron travelling when it reaches the positive plate? (mass of electron = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
working: This energy is gained as kinetic energy: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\)
questions.explanation: The work done by the field, W = Vq = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ J, is gained entirely as kinetic energy ½mv². Solving gives v = 5.9 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (about 5900 km s⁻¹, roughly 2% of the speed of light) — so classical mechanics is fine, no relativity needed.

questions.q: An electric field can be used to increase the speed and kinetic energy of charged particles. In devices such as the mass spectrometer, electron microscope, synchrotron and Large Hadron Collider, what is the first part that produces the charged particles and gives them their initial acceleration?
options: A magnetic lens
An electron gun, in which electrons boil off a hot filament and are accelerated across to a positive plate
A storage ring
A bubble chamber
questions.explanation: An electric field can act as a particle accelerator. The first part of devices like the mass spectrometer, electron microscope, synchrotron and Large Hadron Collider is an electron gun: a hot filament boils electrons off its surface and the electric field pulls them off and accelerates them through a hole in the positive plate to form a beam.

questions.q: From memory: when a charged particle is injected with speed into a uniform field between parallel plates from one side, what is its subsequent motion similar to, and why?
keyPoints: Its subsequent motion is similar to projectile motion (like the vertical motion under gravity).
Across the field there is no force, so that velocity component stays constant; along the field the constant force F = qE gives a constant acceleration.
Combining constant velocity in one direction with constant acceleration in the perpendicular direction traces out a parabola — the electric force plays the role gravity plays for a projectile.
questions.explanation: The textbook notes that a charged particle injected sideways into the field undergoes motion similar to projectile motion. If you recalled the independent components (constant across, accelerating along) and the parabola/projectile analogy, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Recall the five-link cause-and-effect chain ('Find Five Constant Accelerating Paths') used to write the extended response explaining the motion of a charge in a uniform electric field.
keyPoints: Field: a uniform field between parallel plates exists in the gap.
Force: the field exerts a force F = qE on the charge (state sign of charge and field direction).
Constant force: because the field is uniform, the force is constant in magnitude and direction.
Acceleration: by Newton's second law (F = ma) the acceleration is constant.
Path: fired across the field gives a parabola; released from rest or fired along the field gives straight-line acceleration.
questions.explanation: The chain Field then Force then Constant force then constant Acceleration then Path is the spine of the extended response. Markers reward naming each link, not just saying 'the particle accelerates because of the field'.

questions.q: Under what condition does a charged particle in a uniform electric field follow a parabolic path rather than a straight line?
options: Whenever the field is strong enough, regardless of how it is launched
Only if the particle's initial velocity has a component across (perpendicular to) the field; if released from rest or fired along the field it accelerates in a straight line
Only for negative charges; positive charges always go straight
Only when gravity is included in the analysis
questions.explanation: The field always exerts the same constant force in one direction. If the starting velocity is along the field or zero, the path is a straight line of uniform acceleration. If the starting velocity has any component across the field, the constant-velocity (across) plus constant-acceleration (along) combination produces a parabola. What changes is the launch direction, not the field.

questions.q: Explain why a positive charge projected horizontally into a uniform electric field directed downward follows a parabolic path, and account for the change in its kinetic energy. (5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The downward uniform field exerts a constant electrostatic force F = qE on the positive charge in the direction of the field (downward). Because the field is uniform this force is constant, so by Newton's second law the charge has a constant downward acceleration a = F/m. The motion resolves into two independent components: horizontally there is no force, so the horizontal velocity stays constant; vertically the constant force produces uniform acceleration, so the vertical velocity grows steadily from zero. Combining constant horizontal velocity with uniformly increasing vertical velocity traces a parabola — exactly analogous to a projectile under gravity, with the electric force playing the role of gravity. As the charge is displaced downward through a potential difference, the field does work W = qV on it, and with no other significant force this work is converted entirely into kinetic energy, so its ½mv² increases as it falls through the potential difference.

criteria.descriptor: States the field exerts a constant force F = qE (downward for the positive charge) because the field is uniform.
Applies Newton's second law to give a constant acceleration in the field direction.
Resolves into independent components: constant horizontal velocity, uniformly accelerating vertical velocity.
Concludes the combination gives a parabola, analogous to projectile motion under gravity.
Accounts for energy: work W = qV done by the field is converted to kinetic energy ½mv² as the charge falls through the potential difference.

questions.explanation: A full-mark answer walks the Field-Force-Constant force-Acceleration-Path chain and then adds the energy story (work = qV becomes ½mv²). The weak 'it accelerates because of the field' answer names a cause and stops, earning almost nothing.
